lesson.subtitle: Lesson 23 -- The Academic Voice
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Aguinaldo Ballon | Lesson 23 -- The Academic Voice
lesson.grammar_point: attribution and stance in academic English with as X argues, according to and stance adverbs

listenings.text: Every year I read hundreds of articles by lawyers who are starting a doctorate, and the most common problem is not grammar. It is voice. The reader cannot tell who is speaking. Is this your idea, or is it the idea of an author you read last week? Good academic writers make this clear in every paragraph. They cite the source, they use a reporting verb that shows the author's position, such as argues, suggests or contends, and then they add their own stance. For example: as Ostrom argues, local rules can work. Admittedly, her cases were small. However, the finding is robust. Three sentences, three voices, and the reader is never lost.

Thank you for the invitation. My research looks at why some regulatory agencies in Latin America are more independent than others. There is a large body of research on this question, but most of it is about Europe and the United States. According to the classic view, independence comes from the law: fixed mandates, separate budgets. My findings suggest a different picture. In the six countries I studied, the agencies that were independent in practice were not always the ones with the strongest laws. What mattered more was the track record of the first directors. Admittedly, six countries is a small sample, so I would not overstate this result. But I think it challenges the classic view.
